rv.q: This musical version of Thelma & Louise has many things going for it, notably some thrilling songs from alt-country legend Neko Case, a great cast led by Amy Lennox and Rachel Turner, and some sparking dialogue from Callie Khouri.
The music chugs along nicely, but the hypnotic allure of the road gets lost.

The good news, all the same, is that Lennox and Tucker are terrific singers who bring real passion to humdrum lyrics. You still long for them to outwit the authorities as they embark on their mini-crime spree. Their picaresque adventures unfurl on a ...
But, try as it might, the show just can’t match the film’s thrust, depth or stunning ending.
Beyond that, the intention around this musical adaptation of the road movie is entirely perplexing.
Fortunately, with Neko Case in charge of the music and lyrics, the Young Vic’s production is far removed from the usual musical theatre fare offered up in the West End.
Thelma & Louise works as a musical and, more importantly, matters as a comment on why these two made the choices they did.

The overall effect is a solid and occasionally charming musical which eschews whimsy in favour of real life jeopardy, and is a female buddy tale which comes close to emulating the shenanigans of Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid.
There is a considerable amount of anarchic spirit, but it doesn’t go as far as it could or fully embrace what musical theatre has to offer.
The original storytelling still shines through, but the adaptation struggles to match the power of the story it is telling.
What is meant to be something thrilling and captivating instead ebbs and flows, largely because of musical numbers that add little, if anything at all to the narrative.
But it all feels meagre, slow-paced, stripped of excitement and crucially of that sense of liberation which powers the narrative even as it dips towards its inevitable close.
This is storytelling at its best.
It’s funny, emotional, uplifting and defiant – with two phenomenal performances from its brilliant Thelma and Louise.
Thelma & Louise ’s road trip keeps going for ever – but now it’s destined to continue as a terrific musical.
For me, this felt absolutely right for the Young Vic stage and is easily the best new musical I have seen there.
Thelma & Louise is an ambitious production that excels in its atmosphere and storytelling.
Overall, he finds it worthwhile, emotionally potent, and more successful than many recent new musicals.
As Tucker sings of her character's back story beneath a starlit desert sky, the moment is profound and powerful.
Thelma & Louise is far from a total car crash, but it does make you feel as if it has left you lingering in midair waiting for an impact that never came.
With the songs removed and a tighter, shorter script, this could be something really special.
By any other measure, this experiment is a mediocre failure.

Ultimately unable to escape the violent misogyny that leaks into every crevice of their lives, Thelma & Louise does an excellent job at expressing the bleak reality of womanhood under patriarchy while affording Thelma and Louise full autonomy and whole, believable characterisations.
A slick, intelligent and impressively layered production that finds genuinely theatrical ways to tell an iconic road-trip story.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this musical adaptation, with critics praising the strong leads (Lennox and Tucker) and theatrical staging, but questioning whether the score and adaptation match the power of the iconic 1991 film.
